client: I've been really struggling lately with everything going on at work. I'm a project manager, and my team missed a really important deadline last week, and ever since then I just can't seem to shut my brain off — I keep replaying everything, wondering what I could have done differently. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure just keeps building no matter what I do.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy mental load right now — that constant replaying of events can be exhausting, and it makes sense that you're feeling stuck and a bit skeptical that anything will help. That kind of rumination often comes from a place of wanting to regain control, which shows how much you care about your work and your team. I'm curious — when you replay those events, what's the thought that tends to come up most often for you?

client: The thought that keeps coming back is that I should have caught the warning signs earlier — like, there were moments where I sensed things were slipping, but I told myself the team would pull through. And now I just keep thinking, what kind of project manager misses something that obvious? It feels like I failed everyone, my team, my boss, the whole project.
therapist: That thought — "what kind of project manager misses something that obvious?" — sounds like it's hitting you really hard, and it's carrying a lot of weight about your whole identity and worth, not just this one situation. It's worth gently noticing that you *did* sense things were slipping, which actually shows your instincts were working — so I'm wondering if the full picture is a little more complex than "I failed everyone." What do you think was going on at the time that made you decide to trust the team would pull through — was that an unreasonable call given what you knew then?

client: I mean, at the time it didn't feel unreasonable — we'd hit rough patches before and always managed to get through them, and two of my most reliable people told me they had it under control. But I guess what I'm struggling with is that even if it wasn't totally unreasonable, it still went wrong, and I'm the one responsible for the outcome regardless of the reasoning behind my decisions. I hear what you're saying about the full picture being more complex, but it's hard to actually feel that way when my boss is still sending me those short, clipped emails and I'm just waiting for the other shoe to drop.
therapist: You're holding two really difficult things at once — intellectually recognizing that your decision made sense at the time, but emotionally feeling the full weight of the outcome, and that gap between knowing and *feeling* is one of the hardest things to sit with. The uncertainty with your boss is also keeping you in a kind of suspended tension, which makes it really hard for your brain to settle and process things clearly. I'm wondering — when you imagine that "other shoe dropping," what's the specific outcome you're most afraid of, and how likely do you genuinely think that is when you step back from it?

client: Honestly, my biggest fear is that my boss has already mentally checked out on me — like, that she's decided I'm not cut out for this level of responsibility and she's just figuring out how to move me off the bigger projects or maybe let me go entirely. And when I try to step back and assess how likely that actually is, I want to say it's probably not that likely because I've had mostly strong performance reviews, but then my brain just immediately counters with "but this was a really visible failure, and one big mistake can erase all of that." It's like I can't hold onto the reassuring thought for more than a few seconds before the anxiety just pulls me back under.
therapist: That pattern you just described — where the reassuring thought slips away almost immediately and the anxious one rushes back in — is so common, and it tells us that right now your brain is working really hard to protect you from a threat, even if it's overestimating how real that threat is. What's really worth holding onto is that you *were* able to generate that evidence — the strong performance reviews, your track record — which means part of you knows the full picture, even if anxiety keeps drowning it out. I'm curious, if a trusted colleague came to you with this exact situation — same history, same mistake, same fear — what would you actually tell them about whether one visible failure erases everything that came before it?

client: If a colleague came to me with that, I'd probably tell them that one mistake doesn't define their whole career and that everyone drops the ball sometimes, especially on complex projects. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just feels hollow — like I'm just saying words without actually believing them, you know? I think part of me feels like I deserve to be harder on myself than I would be on someone else, because I'm the one who was supposed to be in charge.
therapist: That belief — that you *deserve* harsher judgment because you were in charge — is really worth slowing down on, because it's doing a lot of work underneath all of this. Responsibility for a project is real, but it's different from deserving punishment, and somewhere along the way those two things have gotten tangled together for you. What do you think taught you that being in charge means you're not allowed the same compassion you'd naturally give to someone else?

client: That's a question I wasn't expecting, and it's making me uncomfortable in a way that feels significant. I think maybe it goes back to how I grew up — my dad was really big on accountability, like, "if you take on a responsibility, you own everything that comes with it, no excuses," and I internalized that pretty deeply. But I'm not sure digging into that is going to help me fix what's happening at work right now, because even if I understand where it came from, I still have to face my boss and my team on Monday.
therapist: That discomfort you're feeling is actually really meaningful — it suggests you've touched something important, and it makes complete sense that a message you absorbed so deeply from someone you looked up to would shape how hard you are on yourself today. You're right that Monday is real and pressing, and we don't need to resolve everything about the past to help you walk in there feeling more grounded. So let's connect both — knowing that your inner critic has deep roots might help you hold it a little more loosely this week: what would it look like to face your boss and team on Monday as someone who made a costly but understandable call, rather than as someone who has something to atone for?

client: I like the way you framed that, but I honestly don't know if I can pull it off — like, the moment I walk into that room and see my boss's face, I think all of that reframing is just going to evaporate and I'll be right back in "damage control" mode. I guess what I'm struggling with is that it feels almost dishonest to walk in there acting like I'm not carrying a ton of guilt, because I am, and I don't want to come across as someone who isn't taking the failure seriously enough.
therapist: There's something really honest and even admirable in what you just said — you don't want to perform confidence you don't feel, and you don't want to minimize a real failure, and that actually speaks to your integrity as a leader. But I want to gently offer a reframe: walking in as someone who takes this seriously *and* believes they're still capable isn't dishonest — it's actually the most accurate version of the truth, because both of those things are real. What if "taking it seriously" and "not treating yourself as permanently damaged" aren't opposites, but something you could actually hold together when you walk into that room?

client: When you put it that way, I can almost see how those two things could coexist, but I think the practical challenge is that I don't actually know how to hold both of them at the same time in the moment — like, what does that even look like when my boss is asking me directly what went wrong? I guess I'm also worried that if I walk in with any sense of "I'm still capable," it'll read as defensive or like I'm not fully owning what happened, and that could make things worse with her.
therapist: You're in a much more grounded place than when we started — you're not just spiraling, you're actually problem-solving how to show up well, which is a real shift. When your boss asks what went wrong, owning it fully and demonstrating capability aren't in conflict — something like "here's what I missed, here's what I've learned, and here's what I'd do differently" is both accountable *and* forward-looking, and that combination tends to read as leadership rather than defensiveness. What do you think would feel most important for your boss to hear from you on Monday — what's the one thing you'd want her to walk away knowing?

client: I think the one thing I'd want her to walk away knowing is that I'm not someone who makes excuses and that I've already been thinking hard about what needs to change going forward — not just to protect myself, but because I actually care about the team delivering well. But even as I say that, I notice I'm already rehearsing it in my head like a performance, and I'm worried that if it comes out too polished it'll sound like I'm managing her rather than being real with her. I guess I'm not sure how to be both prepared and genuine at the same time.
therapist: What's really striking is that the thing you want her to know — that you care about the team, not just yourself — is something you genuinely feel, which means it's not a performance at all, it's just the truth. The difference between "managed" and "genuine" often isn't about how polished the words are, but whether they're coming from a real place, and everything you've shared today tells me yours are. What might it feel like to walk in on Monday not with a rehearsed script, but just with that one true thing as your anchor?

client: Honestly, when I sit with that for a second, it does feel a little less terrifying — like, if I'm just holding onto something real instead of trying to get the words exactly right, there's less to mess up. But I think my worry is that one true thing might not feel like enough when I'm actually in the room and she starts asking specific questions about timelines and process breakdowns. I guess I'm not used to trusting that just being genuine is sufficient — it feels like I need to have all the answers ready or I'll look like I'm still not on top of things.
therapist: It sounds like things have softened just a little — and that shift matters, even if the worry about specifics is still there underneath it. Here's something worth considering: knowing your timelines and process details is reasonable preparation, but "having all the answers" and "being genuine" aren't the same thing — and your boss has likely seen enough leaders to know the difference between someone who's genuinely reflective and someone who's just reciting polished answers. What would it mean for you to trust that saying "I'm still working through some of the specifics but here's what I know so far" is actually a sign of being on top of things, rather than a sign of weakness?
